Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

continue with the cream linen only after the lower drain trough has been rinsed and checked", "output": "This is the dye room log for Thursday, the twelfth of June, dictated by Mara Voss at the North Quay Textile Workshop. The morning shift opened the east mixing bay at six forty and checked the two kettle gauges before anyone moved the wool lots. Kettle one held at thirty-eight degrees, and kettle two read thirty-seven and a half. The wall thermometer was three degrees lower, so I asked Dev to check it against the brass hand gauge. He did and wrote that the wall unit was slow, not the kettle dials. The lot on the first trolley was wool flannel from batch W eighteen forty-six, in twelve rolls, with a total dry weight of ninety-six kilos.

The requested shade was Harbor Slate from the April card, but the card had faded on its lower edge, and the small square looked greener under the east window. Mara compared it with the retained sample from the May run and called for the blue-violet concentrate rather than the plain navy. Dev said, “The retained square is closer to the coat lining than the card is,” and I said, “Right,” because that was the reason we kept a control square from May. The mix sheet called for six hundred grams of blue-violet concentrate and one hundred and eighty grams of charcoal concentrate per fifty kilos of dry wool. The scale was checked with the one-kilo brass weight before the first measure. It settled at one thousand grams exactly, and the empty stainless scoop was tared between colors.

First, the wool was wetted in clean water for twenty minutes. The water came from tank three and measured at pH 6.4. After soaking, the crew lifted the rolls one at a time and let each drain for two minutes before loading the kettle. Dev asked whether to add salt with the first concentrate or wait until the dye bath turned over. Mara said, “Add it after the wool is moving, because the folds on this flannel hold color unevenly if the salt goes in too soon.” She pointed to the pale stripe near the selvage on the previous trial roll. That stripe was recorded on Tuesday and was not treated as a stain; it followed a tight fold in the cloth.

The actual first rinse began at eight—no, nine fifteen—after the kettle had held at seventy-two degrees for twelve minutes. The earlier time was my false start from reading the rinse column instead of the dye column. We used the lower drain trough because the upper trough was still carrying the cream linen from the night shift. The valve was turned toward the blue mark, and Dev checked that the cream water had stopped before the wool came through. The rinse took eleven minutes. The outgoing water was still faintly blue at minute eight and clear enough at minute eleven. The crew saved a jar from the first drain and labeled it “Thursday first rinse” for comparison with the next slate run.

At the break, Nico brought over a small card with a note from his aunt, who had worked at a mill near Porto. She had written “tá, fica bom,” meaning “okay, it looks good,” beside a photograph of the blue-gray fabric. He told us tá is what she says when she agrees that a color is acceptable, not when she is hesitating. He was pleased that the new sample matched the photograph more closely than the April card. Dev read the card twice and said he would keep the Portuguese words on the sample sleeve because they explained why Nico had marked the photograph as an approval of the shade, not as a batch instruction. Nobody added the aunt's note to the formula sheet.

1. The first retained swatch is the dry control cut from the left end of roll four and marked with the date and batch number.
2. The second swatch is the wet control taken after the eleven-minute rinse and clipped to the back of the log sleeve.
3. The third swatch is from the right end of roll twelve and is being held for the afternoon light check. Do not sew the three together. The edges are different, and the comparison needs each swatch to remain separate. Dev wrote the same directions on the envelope and used pencil because the outer paper may be replaced.

At ten thirty, Lena from finishing came to check the fabric under the north skylight. She said the face looked slightly cooler there than beside the kettle, but the shade did not shift toward green. She asked if the whole lot should be dried before the shade was signed off. Mara said, “Not yet. Keep two rolls damp until the afternoon check, and dry the other ten on the low rack at forty-five degrees.” Lena noted that the damp rolls were numbers three and nine and tied them with white cord. The condition matters because if either damp roll shows a pale fold after drying, the crew must reopen the dye assessment before the lot is packed. If both match the control squares, they can remain in the regular finishing queue. No one has made that check yet.

On the lower shelf, the team found an older notebook with a line in German from the previous consultant: “Er hängt das Muster um neun ans Fenster.” Dev translated it as, “He hangs the sample by the window at nine,” and explained that um in this sentence means “at nine” rather than “around the window.” The old line referred to a separate cotton trial and was not copied into today's shade record. Mara asked him to keep the notebook open to that page until the archive clerk came because the handwriting on the facing page might identify who had changed the cotton temperature. The entry does not name a person, and Dev left the name field blank.

At noon, the bath log showed a final temperature of thirty-four degrees and a pH reading of 6.7. The used liquor was moved to the marked recovery tank rather than sent to the floor drain, as a sample jar was still being compared with the Tuesday trial. Nico weighed the leftover concentrate containers and recorded two hundred and sixteen grams of blue-violet and sixty-eight grams of charcoal. He returned both lids tightly closed and put the containers on the locked shelf. The scale was wiped dry and checked again with the brass weight before the afternoon team used it. One of the trolley wheels had left a short blue mark near the drain. Lena wiped the floor and added the cleaning time to the room board.

Mara closed this part of the log at twelve twenty. She left the two damp rolls on the low rack with the white cords visible and placed the three separate swatches in a paper sleeve marked “Harbor Slate comparison.” She wrote that the retained May square was the closer color reference than the faded April card and that the blue rinse jar should remain beside the sleeve until the next slate batch is assessed. The afternoon light check is still pending, and the finishing decision for rolls three and nine depends on what the crew sees after drying. The other ten rolls are recorded as drying at forty-five degrees. The archive notebook remains open for the clerk, and the dye room will continue with the cream linen only after the lower drain trough has been rinsed and checked."}]
